query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the HfNbTaTiZr alloy, lattice distortion arising from the atomic size mismatch stabilizes a single-phase BCC structure and sets up high intrinsic stress fields that cause a temperature‐induced change in the dominant dislocation activity—from mainly screw dislocation glide at lower temperatures to edge dislocation–mediated plasticity at elevated temperatures. This transition results in a plateau in elastic moduli and a muted thermal expansion behavior in the high-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, homogeneous single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with minimal segregation.
generation.intervention: High-temperature mechanical testing (tensile and/or compressive) combined with in situ microstructural characterization (e.g., neutron diffraction and TEM) across an elevated temperature range (from approximately 800°C to 1600°C).
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, with controlled strain rates ranging from quasi-static to moderate; temperature increment steps to capture the transition in dislocation behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale lattice distortions and the evolution of dislocation core configurations that govern the switch from screw to edge dislocation activity.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the high lattice friction supports predominantly screw dislocation glide, which gradually becomes thermally activated. As temperature increases, sufficient thermal energy enables a crossover to edge dislocation glide—a mode less sensitive to temperature and more influenced by the severe lattice distortions. This dislocation mode transition limits further reductions in yield strength, produces a plateau in the elastic modulus, and contributes to a lower-than-expected thermal expansion coefficient by reducing lattice anharmonicity.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable plateau or reduced rate of change in both the yield strength and elastic modulus along with a relatively low thermal expansion coefficient over the elevated temperature range. In situ observations should reveal increasing edge dislocation density relative to screw dislocations as temperature rises.
generation.baseline: Room-temperature mechanical properties and thermal expansion behavior of the same alloy as well as conventional BCC refractory alloys that display monotonically decreasing strength and modulus with temperature due to persistent screw dislocation control.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold only for samples maintaining a homogeneous single-phase BCC structure without significant phase segregation or precipitate formation. Deviations may occur if processing or aging induces microstructural heterogeneities.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature at which the dislocation transition occurs and the quantitative contribution of the edge dislocation mechanism to the observed plateau behavior are uncertain; minor compositional fluctuations or processing history may also affect the response.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in situ high-temperature tensile or compressive tests on HfNbTaTiZr samples using neutron diffraction and TEM to monitor dislocation evolution as temperature increases. Simultaneously measure yield strength, elastic modulus, and thermal expansion. Data should be collected at incremental temperatures from 800°C to 1600°C.
measurements: Dislocation type and density (via in situ TEM/neutron diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanical property measurements (yield strength and elastic modulus) do not exhibit a plateau and continue to vary monotonically with temperature, or if in situ observations do not show a transition from screw-dominated to edge-dominated dislocation activity, then the hypothesized mechanism would be falsified.

Microstructure and Room Temperature Mechanical Properties of Different 3 and 4 Element Medium Entropy Alloys from HfNbTaTiZr System

Abstract: Refractory high entropy alloys (HEA) are promising materials for high temperature applications. This work presents investigations of the room temperature tensile mechanical properties of selected 3 and 4 elements medium entropy alloys (MEA) derived from the HfNbTaTiZr system. Tensile testing was combined with fractographic and microstructure analysis, using scanning electron microscope (SEM), wavelength dispersive spectroscope (WDS) and X-Ray powder diffraction (XRD). The 5 element HEA alloy HfNbTaTiZr exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation while 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength. Some of them are ductile, some of them brittle, depending on microstructure. Simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy resulted in a significant reduction of ductility caused by reduction of the BCC phase content. Precipitation of Ta rich particles on grain boundaries reduces further the maximum elongation to failure down to zero values.

Edge-dislocation-induced ultrahigh elevated-temperature strength of HfMoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: ABSTRACTOver 150 refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been proposed in the last decade. Early alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW still show an unparalleled yield strength of approximately 400 MPa at 1600°C. However, RHEAs with even elevated high-temperature strength are necessary in aerospace vehicles and nuclear reactors to cope with advanced technology in the future. Here, solid-solution strengthening calculation and melting point prediction are combined to design single-phase RHEA for attaining ultrahigh strength at 1600°C. The results show that Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW alloys after fully homogeneous treatment at 2100°C for 2 h reveal a homogenous body-centered cubic phase. HfMoNbTaW alloy exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, much higher than that of MoNbTaVW (477 MPa). It is found that a plateau of strength occurs from 800°C to 1200°C, which is important for raising the strength level of RHEAs at high temperatures.
